evaluation.title: Narrate. World's pov seeing one peculiar rising dynasty arranging marriages all around the globe. Th

messages.content:
Narrate. World's pov seeing one peculiar rising dynasty arranging marriages all around the globe. Their members equally intermarrying with currently prosperous families, and with families that are going to obscurity, fading for one or another reason. They don't seek conquest -  in set of decisive actions (not only war), they carved their own domain once, and then saw no need to expand their Archduchy any further. They send their people searching for knowledge: geneology, myths, legends - in paper, oral traditions, rumors, beliefs. They usualy resolve things diplomatically, and the only kind of wars they are participating, are defending. They accept people seeking better life (declining house; these whose royal families got overthrown; these who aren't first in line of succession and probably won't get anything, except claim that they'll never have means to realize; daughters with no dowries, except lineage they didn't know about) (but still not everyone, only these who are listed as famous/notable in modern history). They could offer money and give better promises. They could "buy" marriage from unwilling parent. They don't overpay though - if target is precious only to them, then why give treasures to these who don't value this person? Usually they are happy to get rid of these people anyway, just wondering why would anyone would want to marry them. They don't care about person's position in succession line. They could even invite people seemingly not descending from any famous house (if their origins long forgotten. or if they are from cadet branch of cadet branch [x] times. or if their ancenstor was a bastard of someone notable, what's often forcibly forgotten). They marry families with claims of descending from someone, be it acquired by diligent research(by target family; but dynasty of Archduchy does researches too), masterfully fabricated in past (by target family, not Archduchy - they don't create fake) with money or cunning (when many believe in lie, it becomes thuth), or if their ancestor accomplished deed fitting figure of the past - Archduchy dynasty "senses" if these claims are important to them (in CK all of that can grant dynasty a bloodline). Unlike others, they treat their women not as spare coins or incubators, but with respect, and give time to decide if they like groom chosen for them (dynasty gets wast, so it's easy to eventually find compatible partner). This dynasty also looks for men and women, young or adult, with good qualities and talents (the most lovable traits (congenital, personal, etc) of CK2 and CK3 players, like Genius, Attractive, Strong, Herculean, Pure-Blooded, etc), most gets married to common members of family, and only the best gets groomed, educated, and married into rulling line. They often accept last members of dynasties into family. It's not rare for them to set up matrilineal marriages - they value their women, so it's understandable when after marrying some scion their kids have mother's dynasty name; but sometimes they also marry distant nephews with women of other families, with condition that at least one child has father's dynasty name - it will become part of "mechanism", carry bloodlines further, while other kids could continue mother's lineage. It doesn't bother them much if kids from these unions doesn't their dynasty name, as long as it makes the bloodline continue. Only ruling line demands all kids to carry their dynasty name. And in the end, even making marriages with someone seemingly insignificant, they still look like they are the winners.

(this whole thing is about CK2 player, using all modern knowledge, to hunt for bloodlines to merge into their dynasty, and to have a descent from every famous historical, mythical, cultural house/figure possible. calculating eugenic programms {like Bene Gesserit with their Kwisatz Haderach, but this line is only for comparison}. for a player, using in-game ledgers, it's easy to track bloodlines passing, and see if the person is really carrying a bloodline or not. player chose the most optimal location, setting nice borders in early stages, and now is playing tall. the majority of bloodlines are patrilineal, meaning that they can't be passed through female by normal marriage. matrilineal marriage can be done, allowing matrilineal transfer from both parents, useful when the last member of bloodline is female. marriages inside dynasty, that are meant to slowly merge all collected bloodlines into the rulling branch, happen only between distant members, avoiding incest)

We watched them rise, not like a tide that drowns the shore, but like a mountain pushing up from the earth—sudden, immovable, and strangely content.

In the beginning, the Kings and Emperors of the known world gripped their sword hilts, expecting the inevitable crusade. When a new power carves out a domain with such decisive, terrifying efficiency, the natural next step is expansion. We waited for their legions to cross the rivers, for their banners to cast shadows over our borders.

But the armies never came. They set their stones, fortified their keeps, and simply… stopped.

It baffled the courts of Europe, Asia, and the East. They played the game of nations differently. While we fought over strips of farmland or trade ports, the Archduchy fought a war of ink, whispers, and weddings. They didn't send generals to our capitals; they sent scholars. Men and women with dust on their sleeves and obsession in their eyes, scouring our libraries for genealogies we had long forgotten.

Then came the proposals.

At first, we laughed. They asked for the hands of the irrelevant. They sought the fourth sons of declining houses, the daughters with no dowries save for a family name that hadn't held power in three centuries. They came for the bastards whose origins we had politely agreed to forget.

"Take them," we sneered, counting their gold. "You pay for refuse."

We thought we were swindling them. We sold them a princess whose father had been overthrown and beheaded, a girl living in exile with nothing but the rags on her back. We sold them the "runt" of a ducal litter—a boy with a clubfoot but a sharp mind, or a girl too tall and broad-shouldered to fit the delicate fashions of the court. We scrutinized the coin they gave us, finding it full weight, and wondered why they didn't haggle harder. They never overpaid, but they bought what no one else wanted.

We didn't understand that they were buying seeds.

They treated these "discarded" spouses with a reverence that unnerved us. In the Archduchy, a deposed princess was not a beggar; she was a vessel of the Carolingian blood, or a direct descendant of the Sassanids. They looked at a hedge knight and saw the blood of a Saint or a mythical warlord flowing in his veins. They knew things about our families that we didn't know ourselves—or perhaps, things we had chosen to ignore.

They hunted myths. If a family claimed descent from a sea-god, or a wolf-mother, or a hero who stopped the sun, the Archduchy was there. They didn't care if the claim was forged in the fires of ambition long ago; they seemingly sensed that if enough people believed the lie, the blood carried the power of the truth. They collected ancestors like dragon scales.

And their methods... they were maddeningly patient.

In our lands, a woman is sent to her husband's house and her name is swallowed by his. In the Archduchy, they played with names like pieces on a board. They arranged matrilineal unions with a frequency that scandalized our priests. If they married a daughter to a distant nephew of a foreign king, they might demand the children bear the mother's name. We conceded, because the groom was a third cousin with no inheritance prospects anyway.

"Let the woman have the name," we’d say, "The boy gets a castle and a stipend."

We didn't see the mechanism clicking into place. We didn't see that they were preserving a specific strand of DNA, keeping a legendary bloodline alive within their sphere until it could be woven back into the main tapestry. They didn't care if a child wasn't of the *Ruling* dynasty, as long as the child was in the *court*, in the *system*, available for the next generation of matchmaking.

Decades passed. The "refuse" we sold them had children. And those children were... different.

The Archduchy began to produce humans that made our heirs look like crude sketches. We saw young men with minds that moved like quicksilver, mastering logistics and theology by age twelve. We saw women of Herculean stature and terrifying beauty, leading defensive regiments that broke our raiding parties without breaking a sweat. They were strong, they were genius, they were beautiful.

They bred out the weakness and bred in the legends.

It wasn't just eugenics; it was a consolidation of history. They engaged in a slow, calculated incest—not the brother-sister rot that plagued the Pharaohs or the Habsburgs, but a distant, mathematical weaving of cousins ten times removed. They consulted their ledgers, ensuring the blood did not spoil, only thickened.

Now, we look at their current Archduke, and we feel a primal shiver.

He stands at the balcony of a domain that hasn't grown an inch in a hundred years, yet he looms over the world. We look at his lineage and we weep.

He holds the blood of the Caesars. He is the heir of David, the scion of Ashoka, the descendant of Odin-worshippers and Pirate Queens. He has the blood of the Prophet and the blood of the Crusader. He carries the "claims" of usurped emperors from China and fallen High Kings from Ireland. Every mythical founder, every saint, every legendary warrior—their blood has been siphoned, preserved, filtered through matrilineal tricks and strategic purchases, and poured into *him*.

We realize now why they never conquered us. They didn't need our land. They only needed our history.

We sit on our sprawling, messy empires, plagued by rebellion and mediocrity, while they sit in their manicured garden, terrifyingly tall. We thought we were the players, expanding our borders on the map. We didn't realize they were playing a different game entirely—and they have already won.
